name: Hassan Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, thanks for meeting with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Okay with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, all good. I like talking about this stuff, honestly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader at a big bauxite mine, keeping the haul roads smooth so the trucks don't shake themselves apart. I'm junior, still learning to cut a clean edge, and the leading hand, Tomas, makes me redo sections when I leave ridges. Shifts are twelve hours, seven days on and seven off. On my off week I do small digging jobs with a second-hand mini excavator I bought last year, and I rent a room from my uncle, who runs a small earthmoving business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a bit disappointing, to be honest. I use AI every day for my side jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that AI turned out to be a handy tool for small business, not a job killer. Online I'd post about how I use it for quoting and invoicing, because that part really works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good news, because nothing threatens the mine job. I quote my weekend digging jobs with an AI on my phone, and I still dig every trench myself. I'd keep building the side business slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the grader and get my sign-off on the bigger model next year. I'd put about a third of my weekend money into paying off the mini excavator, so it's mine by next winter. And I'd keep using AI tools to handle the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Things feel under control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you have saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About five months' worth, plus the excavator. Rent's cheap at my uncle's, which helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bauxite prices, maybe, and whether the mine cuts junior roles. But I have the side business, so I'm not scared.

say: AI was a **handy tool** for small business, not a job killer.
He'd post about using it for **quoting and invoicing** his side jobs.
think: It's **good news** for him, because the grader job at the mine isn't threatened.
He'd keep building the **side business** slowly.
do: Get signed off on the **bigger grader** next year.
Pay off the **mini excavator** by next winter.
S0.quote: I quote my weekend digging jobs with an AI on my phone, and I still dig every trench myself.
fieldNote: Daily **AI user** who applies it to his own small business.
**Cheap rent** and a side income make him unusually secure for a junior.
His only worry is **bauxite prices**, cushioned by the side business.

steps.text: Get signed off on the bigger grader next year
Pay off the mini excavator with weekend job money by winter
Keep using AI to write quotes and invoices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one's the most realistic, I reckon. And it's not bad for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that this is a chance for people willing to learn, and that we shouldn't expect the government to fix everything. Online I'd share tips on using AI for small jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the mine will cut some junior roles eventually, and mine might be one. The bauxite mine will buy robots either way, so I'd rather be the bloke who owns a small one than the one it pushes out. The side business could grow into my main job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine to put me on the autonomous haul road training, because someone has to set up the routes for the robot trucks. I'd buy a second small machine, maybe a skid steer, with savings and a small loan. And I'd keep paying off the excavator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like having two horses in the race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a loan risky right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I'd keep it small, like three months' pay, and my uncle would co-sign. He's done this for thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I'm getting ahead of myself. But he also told me once he wished he'd started his own business at my age.

say: This is a real **chance** for people who are willing to learn.
People shouldn't expect **the government** to fix everything.
think: Junior grader roles at the mine may be **cut** eventually, possibly his.
His **side business** could grow into his main job.
do: Ask for **autonomous haul road** training at the mine.
Buy a **skid steer** with savings and a small loan.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, like having two horses in the race.
S1.quote: The bauxite mine will buy robots either way, so I'd rather be the bloke who owns a small one than the one it pushes out.
fieldNote: He treats disruption as a **business opportunity**, in line with free-market views.
His **uncle's experience** backs his plan and his loan.
He accepts **some risk** to his mine job calmly because of the side income.

steps.text: Ask for training on setting routes for autonomous haul trucks
Buy a second-hand skid steer with savings and a small loan
Grow weekend digging jobs with the mini excavator

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast, even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get ready and stop waiting for someone to save them. But I'd also say the speed is a problem, it's not fair on families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the grader job is gone by 2031, and the business gets hard too. Two years is enough to set up a business, but it's not enough to know which business will still exist. If robots can dig trenches, who hires a bloke with a mini excavator?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the skid steer and pay off the excavator fast instead, to get rid of debt. I'd look at whether I can buy into a robot digger or rent one for jobs, so I'm the one using it. And I'd save harder, aiming for a year of costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. For the first time I'm not sure what the right move is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving the area?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the cities have more building work. But my uncle's here, and family matters. I'd rather make it work here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your uncle say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say adapt or die, like he always does. Then he'd ask me to teach him the AI stuff, because he's sixty and terrible with phones.

say: People need to **get ready** rather than waiting to be saved.
The **speed** is still unfair on families.
think: The **grader job** goes by 2031, and the business gets harder.
He doesn't know which **business** will still exist.
do: Hold off on the skid steer and **clear debt** fast.
Look at buying or renting a **robot digger**.
feel: **Anxious**, unsure of the right move for the first time.
S2.quote: Two years is enough to set up a business, but it's not enough to know which business will still exist.
fieldNote: The fast picture shakes even his **confidence**, because robots also threaten his side business.
He shifts from expansion to **debt reduction**.
He'd still rather **own the robot** than compete with it.

steps.text: Pay off the mini excavator loan early
Price up renting a robot digger for trench jobs
Shelve plans to buy the skid steer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and robots by 2034. That's a business plan's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to get ahead if you start now. I'd tell younger guys at the mine to start a side hustle too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's workable. Five years lets me pay off a robot digger before the big companies even finish their pilot. The thinking side, quoting and scheduling, I already let AI do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the grader job until about 2030 and grow the business on weekends. Around 2031, when AGI arrives, I'd look at buying a small autonomous digger, maybe with my uncle. And I'd keep saving for when robots arrive in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like before a big job you've prepared for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big firms undercut everyone with cheaper robots. Small operators might not survive that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever take a government grant for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it's a loan, not a handout. I want to earn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway, and anyone who doesn't plan has only themselves to blame. Maybe I'd say it softer at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty happy. Ten years is time to build something my own kids could take over, robots and all. By 2039 I'd want three or four machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the skid steer next year, then add machines every couple of years. I'd learn to run and maintain the robotic ones as they come. And I'd get married and settle down, maybe in my early thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the future is mine to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Is that a big part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I want a family, a house, a business to pass on. That's what my uncle has, and it's what I'm aiming for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big companies buy up everything and squeeze the small guys. That would be the one thing.

fieldNote: With ten years he expects to **own** the change, not suffer it.

steps.text: Buy a skid steer next year and add a machine every two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to know which business will survive. What would help is cheap loans for small operators to buy new machines, and rules that stop the big firms from squeezing out small guys.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about owning versus working. Most people only think of a job, but some of us want to own the machine. My uncle taught me that a man with his own machine never waits for a boss to call.

headlineQuote: My uncle taught me that a man with his own machine never waits for a boss to call.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old grader** operator at a bauxite mine, renting a room from his uncle.
He runs a **weekend digging business** with a mini excavator and uses AI daily for quotes.
He's **free-market** and traditional, preferring loans and family help over handouts.
In slow pictures he's **calm**, seeing a chance to grow his business.
In **AGI by 2028** he grows anxious, unsure which business will survive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to know which business will survive.
